Psalmist
SAHM-ist
n. (a writer or singer of psalms)
Hebrew zamir, a song or psalm, from zamar, to make music, to strike the strings. The Authorized Version uses psalmist once, in the phrase the sweet psalmist of Israel, spoken of David in his last words.

Biblical Definition

Now these be the last words of David. David the son of Jesse said, and the man who was raised up on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel, said. Four titles are gathered here at the end of a life, and their order repays attention. He is the son of Jesse — an ordinary man with a named father. He is the one raised up on high — lifted by God, not self-made. He is the anointed of the God of Jacob — a king by divine appointment. And last, when everything else has been said, he is the sweet psalmist of Israel. The songs are named alongside the crown, and it is the songs that the covenant people have carried ever since. David immediately states where they came from: the Spirit of the LORD spake by me, and his word was in my tongue. That single sentence is the doctrine of inspiration in the psalmist's own mouth, and it settles what the Psalter is. These are not religious poems that later generations found useful; they are the word of God given through a man, which is why the New Testament quotes them as Scripture and why the church has always sung them. The office was not David's alone — the Psalter carries Asaph, the sons of Korah, Moses, and Solomon — but the title settles on David, and the church's singing has followed his lead ever since: let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): a writer or composer of sacred songs; a title particularly applied to David and other authors of the Scriptural psalms.

expand to see more

PSALMIST, n. A writer or composer of sacred songs; a title particularly applied to David and the other authors of the scriptural psalms.

PSALM, n. A sacred song or hymn; a composition in verse, designed to be sung in the worship of God.

PSALTER, n. The Book of Psalms; a name given to the collection of psalms of David.

ANOINTED, pp. Smeared or rubbed with oil; consecrated by unction; set apart to an office.

INSPIRATION, n. The infusion of ideas into the mind by the Holy Spirit; the conveying into the minds of men, ideas, notices or monitions by extraordinary or supernatural influence.

Key Scripture

2 Samuel 23:1 — "Now these be the last words of David. David the son of Jesse said, and the man who was raised up on high, the anointed of the God of Jacob, and the sweet psalmist of Israel, said,"

2 Samuel 23:2 — "The Spirit of the LORD spake by me, and his word was in my tongue."

Colossians 3:16 — "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord."

Psalm 95:1 — "O come, let us sing unto the LORD: let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation."

Modern Corruption

The Psalms are widely treated as ancient devotional poetry that models honest emotion; David states plainly that the Spirit of the LORD spoke by him, which makes the Psalter revelation and not merely expression.

expand to see more

The devotional reading now standard in many churches treats the Psalms chiefly as a record of human feeling — useful because the psalmist is raw and unguarded, and therefore permission for the reader to be the same. There is a truth in it; the Psalter does give voice to grief, rage, and confusion without tidying them. But David's own account in his last words is that the Spirit of the LORD spake by him and his word was in his tongue. That makes the Psalms God's speech to his people before they are the people's speech to God, and a psalm of lament is not merely permission to complain but instruction in how a covenant man brings his complaint.

The critical reading damages the same doctrine from the academic side, reassigning the Davidic psalms to later editors and post-exilic communities and treating the superscriptions as devotional fiction. The dictionary holds the Davidic authorship of the psalms ascribed to him, as the New Testament does when it argues from David himself saith. And the practical loss from either direction is the same. A church that no longer regards the Psalter as the Spirit's word will sing less of it, and Paul's command that the word of Christ dwell in us richly, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms, quietly goes unobeyed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew zamir (H2158), a song or psalm; zamar (H2167), to make music with strings; mashiach (H4899), anointed; ruach (H7307), Spirit.

expand to see more

Hebrew zamir (H2158) — a song, a psalm; behind the sweet psalmist of Israel.

Hebrew zamar (H2167) — to strike the strings, to make melody; the root of the psalmist's office.

Hebrew mashiach (H4899) — anointed one; rendered the anointed of the God of Jacob.

Hebrew ruach (H7307) — Spirit, breath; the Spirit of the LORD spake by me.

Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm; commanded for the church's singing at Colossians 3:16.

Usage

"“the sweet psalmist of Israel” — the last of David's four titles."

"“the Spirit of the LORD spake by me” — inspiration, in the psalmist's own words."

"“in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” — the church's commanded singing."
